title: Borrowing from rivals
hook: Seneca quotes Epicurus often, taking good ideas from a rival school (Letters 2–29)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the Principal Doctrines, where Epicurus ranked friendship as wisdom's greatest gift. Your line was friendship first.

A fan of one team sits up late studying the rival team's playbook, admiring it, taking notes. Someone deep in one political camp reads the other side's best writer every week. It doesn't happen often, and to some people it looks like betrayal. Reading the other side usually means hunting for what's wrong with it. Seneca, a committed Stoic, did something different, over and over, in his letters to a friend. He kept quoting the founder of the rival school.
screen: `STUDYING THE OTHER TEAM'S PLAYBOOK.` → `IT FEELS LIKE BETRAYAL.` → `SENECA QUOTES THE RIVAL.`

segments.voice: First, the habit. In his early letters to his friend Lucilius, Seneca often ends with a small gift: a saying to take away. And again and again, the saying comes from Epicurus, head of the Garden, the school Stoics argued against on gods, nature, pleasure and death. Second, how he explains it. In Letter 2, Seneca says he likes to cross into the enemy's camp, in Richard Gummere's translation, "not as a deserter, but as a scout." He isn't switching sides. He's going over to bring back what's useful. The gift from Epicurus that day: contented poverty is an honorable state. Third, his principle. Lucilius seems to have teased him about it. Seneca answers, across several letters, that a true and well-said thing belongs to everyone; the best ideas are public property, whoever said them first. He'll take a good line from anyone. Fourth, what he doesn't do. He doesn't pretend the schools agree. He keeps his own Stoic views, and later in the letters he argues hard against Epicurean ideas. Borrowing a good thing isn't the same as giving up your own ground. And respecting a rival's insight isn't the same as pretending your differences don't matter. That's harder than either cheering your side or abandoning it: holding your convictions and keeping your ears open, at the same time.
screen: `A GIFT AT THE END OF EACH LETTER.` · `NOT A DESERTER, BUT A SCOUT.` · `A TRUE THING BELONGS TO EVERYONE.` · `BORROW WITHOUT GIVING UP GROUND.` · then, large: `BORROW THE GOOD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you disagree with, a relative, a writer, a coworker, and let the disagreement be there without resolving it. Then, like a scout, look for one thing they get right: one value, one insight, one fair point. When you find it, hold it up and look at it, without giving up anything of your own.
Explorator. Seneca's word for himself crossing into Epicurus's camp: not a deserter, but a scout bringing back what's useful. Today's word.
Your line: borrow the good. A true, well-said thing belongs to everyone. Day six hundred fifty-four, done.

howItsDone: Readers of Seneca's letters notice how often he closes with a saying from Epicurus, and many take it as a model for learning from rival views while keeping one's own.

original.note: Latin: a scout. Seneca crosses into the enemy's camp not as a transfuga, a deserter, but as an explorator.

chat.says: Why would a committed Stoic like Seneca keep quoting Epicurus, his rival?
options: He crossed over as a scout: a true, well-said thing belongs to everyone.
He had quietly switched sides and become an Epicurean in later years.
He quoted Epicurus only to mock him and show where he went wrong.
chat.meaning: Seneca went over "not as a deserter, but as a scout." He kept his Stoic views and took good lines from anyone.
